The 5th part of laissez-faire ideology is that in a free market economy, everybody gets their just rewards. The rich earn their wealth, and the poor, they earn their poverty. The system is just. words: OK, yeah. I, I'm going to back up to the, the, um, late 19th century to build a more complete answer to this essential question. So, once work was inside of factories, people on the outside could no longer see how hard. How diligently, how well the worker worked. It came to be known by everybody that inside the factory, they were just appendages of machines. They were just working according to the clock, they were working according to the regularity of the machines, and they had no control over the work, and consequently, there was much, not much to appreciate about Their work, of them as workers, as a matter of fact, it was rather negative, they were being bossed about, and uh all the control over their work was taken away, they were alienated. They could squeeze down inequality, dramatically Prove the quality of work. Great worker power, but the power was not realized because the ideology of the wealthy laissez-faire ideology still remained adequately powerful that worker to convince the workers that such reforms would not really be in their benefit, so workers didn't use their political muscle to do what essentially they could have done. By the way, they only began to do that in the 1930s during the Great Depression, when social work and living conditions became so awful that laissez-faire ideology was partially delegitimated. The resurgence of laissez-faire ideology that we discussed in just, uh, just a moment ago. Respect and self-respect for the quality of the work life they had, or for the contributions to community because they lived in slums, there was no real community in the traditional sense. Goods. It was advocated by Franklin Delano Roosevelt in the 1930s to be part of the Social Security Act. It was advocated again to be the Full Employment Act of 1946. This is the most substantial act that could be in, could be put in place which would raise the quality of life of the working class. And note that. Employers in the private sector would have to offer work of an equal quality, equal pleasantness, and pay to attract people from the guaranteed employment program, which is offering wages, incomes at living wages with benefits. So essentially it would raise. The quality of work and decrease dramatically insecurity in our society. So that's, that's one piece of what my book is proposing. The second is workplace democracy. Workplace democracy would be where workers own and democratically control. The firms, the businesses in which they work. They would essentially, we would essentially be extending democracy from the political realm into the world of work. In a firm owned and controlled by its workers, nobody would take orders from anybody that they had not participated in electing. So the people that are elected. To organize, to direct activities within the business, because you do need some hierarchy and organization for firm firm efficiency. You can't have everybody meeting to simply determine every decision. That would be inefficient and rather stupid. Instead. SELECT people to do the organizing, but they are your servants, and they are elected by you and for a term of office, they run for office again if they choose, and you don't have to elect them again if they didn't do well, and if they really mess up badly, you could put into your constitution. Means to impeach them, just like in the political world, get them out. So, essentially, workers then would control their firms, and that they would, they would do so in community with all other workers. There is some argument amongst those people that support this formula for work, that it would be more efficient, and it would be more efficient for two major reasons. One is that workers would all be monitoring each other, that it, it wouldn't be supervisors and bosses, it would rather be everybody has an interest in all other workers. Working diligently and well. So, and they would have interest, everyone, in working hard, because all of the benefits of the work would come to them, either as wages or as increase in the value of their ownership shares. So the second reason then, is that every worker would have an interest in every other worker being as skilled as possible. Now that is in contrast with a typical capitalist workplace today. In a typical capitalist workplace today, you don't want the other workers to be better than you because if somebody gets fired, it's gonna be you if they're better. So, rather than face that, You would want all of your co-workers to be highly educated, highly skilled, and you would do what you could to help advance that. For these two reasons, then, many people believe that the economy would actually be more efficient, that it would work better. Through consumption, which doesn't work. It just puts us in competition with each other for status, in which we ruin our environment as we all consume evermore. We're all on a treadmill, running faster, but not becoming any better off for it. And it would take us from that world to a world in which people would get fulfillment, meaningfulness, they would become. Essentially members of a strong community of the workplace, and let's note that communities outside their work would become stronger because worker-owned firms would have no incentive to move to where wages are cheaper. They would have no incentive to move the, the production facilities to Mexico or to Korea or wherever else. Work is cheaper and environmental standards are lower. So because they would have no incentive in moving their firms, the community in which they lived would have greater stability, and they would come to have greater interest in investing in their communities, making community life richer, and essentially, people would be able to get their meaningfulness. Their social status from participating in work where no one bosses them about and in community life. So not that consumption doesn't remain important. I like. My flat screen television. I like consumer goods. It's not that consumer goods are bad, they're not. They're wonderful. It's not that economic growth should even end. It's instead that economic growth should become benign in terms of the environment, that it should no longer be the goal which we pursue, sacrificing other values to get there. That is, we shouldn't pursue endlessly economic growth and ever greater consumption, sacrificing meaningful, fulfilling work, community, rich communities. Our environment. And suffering stress, and pessimism about our lives.

Well, no one knows the answer to that, but I would, I would mention this.
